title: Can One Person Attend All the Meetings?

concept.title: Sort the meetings by their start: only neighbours in this order can clash
body: A person has `n` meetings; the meeting `i` lasts from `start` until `end`, and the person cannot be in two meetings at the same time. A meeting that ends at the moment 10 and one that starts at the moment 10 do **not** clash (the time is a half-open range: it includes the start and excludes the end). Can the person attend all the meetings? For `(0, 30) (5, 10) (15, 20)` no: the meeting `(0, 30)` covers the other two. For `(7, 10) (2, 4)` yes.

Comparing every pair is O(n^2). Instead **sort the meetings by the start time**. If two meetings clash, then the meeting that starts first is still running when the second starts; and if some pair clashes, then a pair of **neighbours** in the sorted order clashes too (the meeting with the latest end so far reaches the next start, and the neighbour is a clash by itself or an earlier one already is). So scan the sorted list and compare each start with the **end of the previous meeting**: if `start < previous end`, there is a clash.

body.code:
meetings.sort()                         # by the start time
prev_end = 0
ok = True
for start, end in meetings:
    if start < prev_end:                # this meeting starts before the previous one ends
        ok = False
        break
    prev_end = end
print("yes" if ok else "no")

body: Sorting costs O(n log n) and the scan O(n). Because the scan stops at the first clash, and each meeting only has to be compared with the previous one, no pair is ever compared twice. "Sort by start, then walk with the latest end" is the pattern for almost every interval problem in this part.

statement: A person has `n` meetings; the meeting `i` takes the time from `start[i]` up to, but not including, `end[i]`. A person can attend a set of meetings only if no two of them overlap in time (a meeting may start exactly when another one ends). Print `yes` if the person can attend all the meetings, otherwise `no`.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`: the number of meetings.
Each of the next `n` lines has two numbers `start` and `end`: the meeting takes the time from `start` up to (but not including) `end`.

examples.note: The first meeting lasts from 0 to 30 and clashes with the others: no.
The meetings do not overlap: yes.

hints: Sort the meetings by their start time.
Compare the start of each meeting with the end of the previous one in the sorted order.
A start equal to the previous end is allowed.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
meetings = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(n)]

# Your code here

explanation: The meetings are sorted by their start; scanning them in this order, a clash exists exactly when some meeting starts before the end of the previous one. The answer is yes if the scan finds no such meeting.
solution.complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
meetings = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(n)]

meetings.sort()
prev_end = 0
ok = True
for start, end in meetings:
    if start < prev_end:
        ok = False
        break
    prev_end = end
print("yes" if ok else "no")
